transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Ava from Redwood, AE on the account. We have Diego (SE) and Priya (Product) with me. Horizon, want to do quick intros?
[00:12] Maya Patel: Hi all, Maya here, ML lead at Horizon. Samir and Lena are here too. We want to see tradeoffs for quantization, particularly INT8 and FP8, since our inference costs are spiking.
[00:24] Diego Morales: Great, thanks. We'll run through the Optimize console, show profiling for INT8/FP8, and then share some benchmark numbers. We'll call out where quality regressions happen and mitigation strategies.
[00:40] Priya Rao: Quick note: we'll reference the benchmark spreadsheet after the demo; we'll send it after the call.
[00:48] Samir Khan: Sounds good. Our constraint: 95th pctl latency < 250ms for short prompts and throughput of ~200 qps.
[01:05] Diego Morales: Noted. We'll map those SLOs to expected latency numbers per quant level. To start, very briefly, INT8 is more aggressive quantization on weights, usually more cost savings but higher quality risk. FP8 keeps a small floating exponent so often better quality with modest latency improvement versus FP16.
[01:35] Jordan Lee: Quick dumb question — is FP8 supported on all hardware? We run mixed GPU fleet.
[01:41] Ava Chen: Great question. FP8 support depends on runtime and hardware; Redwood Optimize will recommend profiles that match your target hardware. For some older GPUs we fall back to INT8 variants or hybrid kernels. We also do kernel selection during compilation.
[01:58] Maya Patel: Can you show the console and the profile comparison?
[02:05] Diego Morales: Sure — sharing screen. (screen noise) Here is the Optimize dashboard; on the left we have model profiles, and on the right the quality-vs-latency matrix.
[02:20] Diego Morales: For this demo we used a customer-like Llama-2-13B-ish model and three prompt classes — "short assistant reply", "multi-turn context", and "structured extraction". We ran baseline FP16, INT8 and FP8.
[02:38] Diego Morales: The chart shows avg latency reduction: INT8 ~2.5x speedup vs FP16 for generation up to 128 tokens; FP8 ~1.8x. But quality delta (measured by ROUGE / exact match on extraction tasks and human scoring on responses) shows INT8 drops ~6-9% on extraction exact-match for tricky numeric answers, FP8 drops ~2-3%.
[03:05] Lena Ortiz: That extraction drop is concerning — we have a billing-reconciliation feature that needs exact fields. How do you mitigate?
[03:12] Diego Morales: Two strategies: hybrid quant profiles and selective fallback. Hybrid means keep critical layers in FP16 or using per-channel quantization for those weights. Selective fallback is policy-level: if confidence low or pattern detected, route that request to FP16 instance.
[03:30] Maya Patel: How much cost/latency hit for fallbacks?
[03:35] Diego Morales: Depends on your fallback policy. If 5% of requests fallback, cost impact is roughly 5-8% more than fully-quantized baseline, but it preserves quality for those edge cases. Latency for the fallback requests will be FP16 latency, but overall 95th pctl may be driven by those; we can do async rechecks for non-blocking use-cases.
[03:58] Samir Khan: For our use-case, we need strict pctl — can't have spikes. Do you offer dedicated pools?
[04:05] Ava Chen: Yes, Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and SLOs. You can configure autoscaling and overflow routing. For POC we usually provision a small dedicated pool so you can test at realistic load without noisy neighbors.
[04:22] Jordan Lee: Diego, can you show the raw numbers for our prompts?
[04:27] Diego Morales: On the spreadsheet — baseline FP16 avg latency 120ms; INT8 48ms; FP8 68ms for short prompts. For multi-turn long contexts (512 tokens) FP16 420ms, INT8 170ms, FP8 230ms. Quality: extraction exact-match FP16 96%, FP8 94%, INT8 89% on that dataset.
[04:55] Maya Patel: The latency improvement is compelling but 89% exact-match on INT8 is borderline. If we selective quantize only encoder layers or specific heads can that improve?
[05:05] Diego Morales: Yes, selective quantization per-layer can recover some of the loss. Our Optimize tooling can generate per-layer sensitivity maps and suggest profiles — e.g., quantize non-critical attention heads to INT8 and keep critical MLP layers in FP8 or FP16.
[05:25] Priya Rao: Also note we can recommend sequence-length aware kernels; many of the regressions come from tokenization/alignment issues, not pure weight quantization.
[05:40] Lena Ortiz: What about safety and hallucination — does quantization increase that?
[05:45] Diego Morales: It can, in edge cases. Human scoring showed slight uptick in hallucination rates for INT8 on open-ended prompts. FP8 was closer to FP16. For production, we recommend FP8 if quality is prioritized, or hybrid profiles with fallback rules.
[06:05] Maya Patel: Any chance to run a head-to-head on our exact prompts?
[06:09] Ava Chen: That's the plan — next step is for you to send canonical prompts and we'll run regression tests and include human evals for extracted fields. We'll also include recommended quant profiles tuned for your workload.
[06:21] Samir Khan: Security question — can PII be kept in our VPC? We need KMS and audit logs.
[06:28] Ava Chen: Yes, Redwood Private can run in your VPC or on-prem; we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and provide audit logs. For Dedicated we also offer VPC peering and encryption at rest. We'll include the security one-pager.
[06:42] Jordan Lee: For benchmarking, do you support 200qps sustained?
[06:46] Diego Morales: We can simulate your load in the POC. INT8 will give you higher throughput but watch out for 95th pctl spikes. We'll include burst capacity recommendations.
[06:57] Maya Patel: Can you explain the quality-vs-latency matrix again?
[07:02] Diego Morales: Sure — X axis latency (lower right is faster), Y axis quality (higher up is better). Each profile sits somewhere on the plane. FP16 sits top-left (high quality, higher latency), FP8 in middle-top (good quality, decent latency), INT8 bottom-right (fast, lower quality). The console can show iso-cost lines, too.
[07:25] Ava Chen: Also, Optimize can recommend profiles by objective — e.g., minimize cost subject to >95% exact-match, or minimize p95 latency subject to acceptable quality threshold.
[07:36] Lena Ortiz: What's the integration effort for our infra? We use private VPC and SSO.
[07:42] Priya Rao: For Private deployment we do a short on-site or partner-assisted install; SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported; audit logs and KMS integration are standard enterprise features. For Dedicated we manage the control plane and you get network isolation.
[07:58] Jordan Lee: Any gotchas with mixed GPU fleet? We have some A100s and some older T4s.
[08:03] Diego Morales: The runtime compiles per node and picks kernels accordingly. For older GPUs that don't support FP8 you either run INT8 or FP16. Optimize will surface recommended routing policies so requests are routed to compatible nodes.
[08:18] Maya Patel: Ok let's talk pricing quickly — how much does quantization save?
[08:22] Ava Chen: Ballpark: INT8 can reduce per-token compute cost ~40-60% depending on model; FP8 around 20-35%. Combined with caching and batching often yields bigger wins. We'll include cost modeling in the spreadsheet.
[08:37] Samir Khan: For our numbers that could be millions annually, so worth validating.
[08:42] Diego Morales: We'll also run a sensitivity analysis: cost vs quality vs p95.
[08:49] Maya Patel: What about regression alerts if quality drops after model updates?
[08:53] Priya Rao: Redwood Optimize ties into eval suites and can set thresholds. If a quant or model update causes regression on your golden prompts, it triggers an alert and we can auto-rollback or pin the model.
[09:06] Jordan Lee: Can you do canary for quant profile rollouts?
[09:09] Diego Morales: Yes, traffic split, canary windows, and automatic fallback on quality regressions are supported.
[09:16] Ava Chen: Quick pause — any other technical deep-dive areas you want us to cover in the POC?
[09:21] Maya Patel: We'd like to see per-layer sensitivity, head-level diagnostics, and an A/B test plan for the billing-recon pipeline. Also, a clear definition of acceptance criteria.
[09:32] Ava Chen: Noted. We'll include that in the POC plan.
[09:36] Samir Khan: Timeline — can you turn around the benchmarks in three days?
[09:40] Ava Chen: Yes, Diego and I will deliver the spreadsheet and initial recommended profiles by 2026-05-18.
[09:47] Diego Morales: One more demo item — here's a screenshot of the per-layer sensitivity map (screen noise). It highlights attention layers that are sensitive to INT8. You can toggle suggested profile and preview expected accuracy drop and latency.
[10:05] Maya Patel: Nice UI. Do you export configs for deployment?
[10:08] Diego Morales: Yes, you can export quant profiles as JSON and apply via the Redwood CLI or the Console; we also have terraform providers for Dedicated infra.
[10:17] Lena Ortiz: For the POC, what are checkpoints?
[10:20] Ava Chen: Kickoff, initial benchmarks within 3 days, mid-POC load test, QA/acceptance on canonical prompts, and final recommendations. We'll propose a 3-week POC by default.
[10:32] Jordan Lee: Any risks we should plan for?
[10:35] Priya Rao: Risk: quality regression on rare prompt patterns — mitigated by selective fallback and human-in-the-loop checks. Another is hardware compatibility — mitigated by routing and hybrid kernel support.
[10:48] Maya Patel: OK let's summarize next steps.
[10:52] Ava Chen: Recap: Redwood to send benchmark spreadsheet and security one-pager; Horizon to share canonical prompts and latency budget; schedule POC kickoff week of 2026-05-25.
[11:05] Samir Khan: Agreed. Thanks all.
[11:09] Ava Chen: Thank you — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the files.
[11:14] (meeting ends)
